body.text: Recent Democratic victories in midterm Congressional elections in the United States should significantly affect U.S. foreign policy in the Asia-Pacific. While President Donald Trump, as executive, continues to be in charge of foreign and military policy, under the U.S. Constitution, Congress – the Senate and the House of Representatives – has significant authority in foreign policy that the Democratic majority will seek to exercise once the new Congress is sworn in on January 3, 2027.

The Trump administration’s foreign policy in the Asia-Pacific writ large has essentially been an afterthought to what it perceives as the China-U.S. confrontation, its ideological commitment to tariffs, and opposition to what it perceives as free-riding on U.S. security guarantees, military expenditures, and open economy by other countries. In the Asia-Pacific, this policy has been less than successful and has alienated allied leadership and populations as well as degraded American hard and soft power without checking Chinese power and influence.

With its large majorities in both Houses, Democratic Congress can have significant influence on this policy in the Asia-Pacific. Given the recent widespread rebuke of the Trump administration and the unpopularity of its policies, Trump will be unable to maintain party-line Republican member support, undermining his ability to use the veto to stop legislation. This could be particularly important as Congress is likely to impose restrictions on the president’s use of force through the War Powers Act or take away his authority to levy tariffs, which is a power delegated to Congress under the constitution.

Perhaps more immediately, both the House and Senate must approve all spending, and imposed conditions to fund certain government activities and sanction a particular type of obligation or expenditure can preclude spending on certain activities or reverse executive actions. For example, after President Barack Obama indicated his willingness to close Guantanamo Bay prison, Congressional Republicans included a measure – opposed by Obama – that prohibited the use of funds to close the prison in a larger defense bill. It can be expected that the use of this spending authority to change administration policy will significantly increase.

The U.S. Senate approves international treaties and presidential appointments, as well as judicial and diplomatic positions. Without Senate confirmation, the inability to fill positions can significantly impact presidential objectives and policy as well as the tone of American relations with particular countries. This authority has already impacted the administration’s agenda, with over 150 nominees awaiting Senate confirmation or further action as of the November election.

Congress also has extensive authority to exercise oversight – investigating government malfeasance as well as substantive procedural and financial (mis)management. With a majority, the Democrats will have the power to initiate investigations into any problem they think fit to address through legislation. These investigations will significantly impact the administration’s personnel, conduct, and policy choices, even though the White House is developing an adversarial position toward oversight by the new Congress.

Current security and economic policy in the Asia-Pacific will be impacted as Congress exercises its oversight into areas like military readiness and policy, the elimination of USAID and the now defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), trade policy, security breaches, corruption, and Taiwan relations.

Finally, Congress can pass simple (House or Senate) or concurrent Congressional Resolutions that are not presented to the president for his signature but rather reflect the sense of Congress, or the sentiments of a chamber on various domestic and foreign policy issues. While not law, resolutions can have political, policy, and normative impact.
Three specific areas of Asia-Pacific policy are likely to be addressed by the Democratic majority in the new year.

First, a Democratic Congress, along with a number of GOP lawmakers less constrained by Trump’s popularity, will underline support for Taiwan and other Asia-Pacific allies and friends in the face of his transactional approach to the region. In May 2026, ahead of a summit between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, incoming Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer warned the Trump administration not to “sell out Taiwan” in exchange for Chinese investment and trade. Similarly, Representative Hakeem Jeffries, who is the favorite for the next speaker of the House, noted the importance of the South Korea-U.S. alliance.

Even Republican legislators have at times pushed back on Trump’s Asia-Pacific policy. For example, Senator Mitch McConnell argued in February that “we need to stop the practice by multiple administrations of picking trade fights with our closest and strongest allies.” With the president’s approval ratings hitting rock bottom, more members of Trump’s own party may be inclined to break ranks with the administration to bolster the traditional Republican policy of supporting U.S. alliances. This congressional support will not only be rhetorical but will also include additional security and economic measures that assist regional allies and friends,

Congressional leaders are also likely to object to any further efforts to cultivate Chinese, North Korean, and Russian leaders at the expense of traditional allies. Republican senators have already been questioning Trump’s invitation of Russian President Vladimir Putin to the Group of 20 (G20) summit in Miami in December. And at the recent Trump-Xi summit in Washington, GOP lawmakers called on Trump to confront Xi over reports that China has provided military assistance to Iran and demanded that China produce real concessions on trade, especially U.S. agricultural exports. Senator Lisa Murkowski said the 21-gun salute and B-1 bomber flyover that greeted Xi’s arrival were “over the top” and inappropriate.

Trump’s meeting with both Xi and Putin on November 19 will be a focal point for incoming legislators from the Republican and Democratic parties alike. Republican Rep. John Moolenaar, the chair of the House Select Committee on the Strategic Competition Between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, said in a speech on November 16 that Trump “doesn’t need a ‘deal’” with Xi. “CCP would just love dialogue, dialogue, dialogue and just keep doing their thing. I would encourage him [Trump] to keep building relationships with like-minded allies and partners,” Moolenaar said.

Second, it is likely that tariffs will be lowered or eliminated either directly through political pressure or through the budget process. According to the Tax Foundation, Trump’s tariffs cover approximately 54 percent of goods imported into the U.S. The most sweeping tariffs now in place are being levied against dozens of countries, many in the Asia-Pacific, for alleged “forced labor” practices.

There is broad domestic dissatisfaction with these tariffs, and their cynical imposition on states without investigation has undermined regional goodwill. Many new Democratic members have been elected to Congress due to the hardship the policy has had on consumers and agricultural and manufacturing sectors. Senator Ron Wyden, the expected chair of the Senate Finance Committee, indicated he was “already talking” about legislation to address the tariffs.

Third, congressional leaders will use their budgetary authority and the media alike to push back against the administration’s transactional approach to international relations, and counteract the growing perception in the region that the United States is not a reliable partner. These efforts to restore U.S. reliability have been helped by the overwhelming rejection of Trump and the Republican Party in the elections, suggesting that the “America First” policies of the administration are not supported by a majority of the population. Part of this can be done through a reestablishment of instruments of commercial and soft power such as USAID and Voice of America. Other efforts could include emphasizing critical minerals cooperation and recommitting to international climate change efforts through the budget process.

Of course, given Trump’s history of ignoring and circumventing legal restrictions, the midterm losses could lead the president to double down and not moderate his agenda. From this perspective, despite congressional efforts, U.S. policy will continue to be shaped by Trump’s “unilateralist, neo-imperial, protectionist, and anti-immigrant impulses,” as Charles Kupchan put it in an article for the Council on Foreign Relations.

Nevertheless, Congress has the institutional means and constitutional authority to resume its role as an independent policymaker as well as the country’s foremost forum for addressing political, economic, and social issues. The fact that Trump policies have been overwhelmingly rebuked by voters and will be opposed by large Democratic majorities in the next House and Senate will revive the interbranch rivalry and competition that has been absent in the past two years of friendly Republican majorities.

Moreover, the potential for even larger Democratic gains in 2028 make continued Republican support of the administration’s policies unlikely, despite the appointment of hardline GOP members to minority leadership positions. In any event, even without Republican support, Democratic control of the budget, oversight and appointments provides an institutional counterweight and a new start for U.S. Asia-Pacific policy.
